title: Don't scan random QR codes
revealText1: These are technical details your browser automatically sent just because you scanned a QR code and opened this page. A QR code is not just an image. It is a gateway that can lead anywhere – and every page you open learns at least this about you:
whyTitle: Why scanning random QR codes is risky
whyList: A QR code can lead to a fraudulent website or phishing page.
It can trigger a download of a malicious file.
It can trick you into logging into a fake service — or logging someone else into your account.
It can be placed over an original legitimate QR code.
You cannot know where it leads until it's too late – at least not on Android.
geoNote: Geolocation and internet provider are determined from the IP address via Cloudflare – accuracy at country level.
nocookiesText1: This page uses no cookies, no trackers, no third-party analytics tools.
nocookiesText2: The goal of this project is to show how easily any website can collect technical information about your device – without any consent or interaction.
motivationText: People often scan QR codes automatically, without thinking. This project was created as a simple, visual demonstration of what you reveal just by scanning a QR code.
contactText: If you're interested in extending this project, integrating it into training, or building your own security awareness campaign, feel free to reach out at info@neskenuj.me
trainingText: …check out the professionals at BOIT Cyber Security, who deliver engaging and practical training in cybersecurity, phishing, social engineering, and safe online behaviour.
bannerDesktop.title: Looks like you're on a computer
bannerDesktop.text: QR codes are mostly scanned on mobile — that's fine. Statistics count desktop and mobile separately, so this visit will show up under Desktop. If you still care about what you reveal, read on — it applies to every device.
bannerBot.title: Automated access detected
bannerBot.text: It looks like this page is being visited by a bot or automated tool. This visit will not be counted in statistics, but is logged for audit purposes.
bannerReturning.title: We recognised you
bannerReturning.text:
You've visited this page once already today. We recognised you by your device fingerprint — no cookies, no login, no interaction required.
This is exactly what any website can do.
faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.q1: What is a fingerprint and how is it created?
faq.q2: How is device type determined (mobile vs. desktop)?
faq.q3: Why is Apple OS data inaccurate?
faq.q4: What are bots and why do I see them in data?
faq.q5: How to protect yourself from QR code tracking?
faq.q6: Can you tell where a QR code leads before scanning?
faq.q7: Do you know where I live? How do you know my city and internet provider?
faq.q8: Is this data really cookie-free and GDPR-friendly?
lang.label: English
faq.a1:
A fingerprint is a unique identifier of your device and browser. It is created by combining dozens of technical parameters — screen resolution, language, time zone, GPU type, number of CPU threads, and more. None of these parameters alone is enough to identify you, but their combination is statistically very unique. The result is hashed using SHA-256 into a 64-character string. This fingerprint contains no personal data, but allows recognising a returning visit from the same device.

How unique are you really?
This page can tell if you've visited before today — but we don't compare you against others. If you're curious how unique your fingerprint is among millions of global users, check out amiunique.org — an academic research project that analyses browser fingerprint uniqueness and shows how easily you can be identified without cookies.

Note: Fingerprints differ between browsers — Chrome and Safari on the same device will produce different fingerprints. Cross-browser identification without additional data is therefore unreliable.
faq.a2: Detection happens in three layers directly in your browser. First, the modern User-Agent Client Hints API is tried, which provides accurate information. If unavailable, the User Agent string is analysed (containing words like "Android" or "iPhone"). As a fallback, the number of touch points is checked — a device with more than one touch point is likely mobile. The result is always an estimate, not an absolute truth. Tablets may be classified differently depending on browser settings.
faq.a3: Safari has intentionally frozen the exact OS version in the User Agent since version 13. This is a privacy protection measure — the precise OS version is one of the signals used for fingerprinting. In practice, this means all Safari users look nearly identical to websites. Basic distinction between iOS, macOS, and Windows is usually preserved, but exact system versions are unreliable for all Apple devices.
faq.a4: Bots are automated programs that browse websites — search engine crawlers, security scanners, or testing tools. Their visits would skew statistics because they don't represent real people. We detect them using several signals: the navigator.webdriver flag (present in Selenium and Puppeteer), suspicious words in the User Agent (headless, crawler, bot), or zero hardware values typical of headless environments. Bots are logged for audit purposes but are not counted in the statistics.
faq.a5:
Before scanning, check whether the QR code hasn't been covered by another one. If your browser shows you the URL before opening it, read it — fraudulent sites often have similar but different domains (e.g. paypa1.com instead of paypal.com). Use private/incognito mode for unknown QR codes. If you want to minimise what you reveal, use a VPN — it masks your real IP address and replaces it with the VPN provider's address.
Short URL preview tricks:
bit.ly — add + to the end: bit.ly/abc123+
TinyURL — add preview. before the domain: preview.tinyurl.com/abc123
Other shorteners — paste the link into checkshorturl.com
faq.a6:
It depends on your device and the app you use to scan.

🍎 iPhone (iOS)
The native iPhone camera automatically shows the URL as a notification before you tap it — just point at the code. You can see the domain the QR points to and decide whether to open it. This is one of the few situations where iOS users have a security advantage over Android.

🤖 Android
The native Android camera in most cases directly shows and opens the URL — without the option to read it first. Behaviour varies by manufacturer (Samsung, Google Pixel, Xiaomi…) and system version. Generally, Android does not offer this protection by default.

🔒 How to protect yourself on Android
Use a dedicated QR code scanning app that shows the URL before opening — for example QR & Barcode Scanner by Gamma Play, or Google Lens (shows URL but immediately offers to open it). Alternatively, you can use the Google Lens function directly in Chrome's address bar on Android.

⚠️ Watch out for shortened URLs
Even if you can see the URL, it may be shortened via bit.ly, tinyurl, or similar services. The domain preview alone is then not enough — anything could be hiding behind a shortened URL. Watch for multiple redirects too — a shortened URL may lead to another shortened URL before reaching the actual destination.
faq.a7:
Yes, approximately. We determine your city and internet provider (ISP) from your IP address — your browser sends it to every website automatically, without exception and without any way to disable it. It is a technical foundation of the internet.

Cloudflare, through which this site runs, translates the IP address into an approximate location (city, region, country) and the provider name (ASN — Autonomous System Number). We receive this data automatically with every request — without an external API, without fees, and without storing the IP address itself.

What we don't store: We intentionally do not log the IP address itself — we only store derived data (city, country, ISP). An IP address is personal data under GDPR; city and ISP are aggregated information that cannot be used to identify a specific person.

Accuracy: IP-based geolocation is approximate — typically at city level, but may be off by tens of kilometres. A VPN or Tor will show the location of the exit node, not your actual location.
faq.a8: Yes — the page stores no cookies and uses neither Google Analytics nor any other third-party trackers. The fingerprint is created and hashed exclusively in your browser; only the resulting hash (not the raw data) is sent to the server. The hash cannot be used to reconstruct the original values. The stored data (hash + device type + timestamp) contains no personal data under GDPR. The goal of this project is precisely to show what websites can do — and to encourage greater awareness.
fp.section.general.title: General information
fp.section.general.desc: Basic data your browser sends automatically with every page load. This information requires no consent and is available to every website.
fp.section.device.title: Device information
fp.section.device.desc: Technical parameters of your device that help websites optimise content — but can also be used to identify a specific device.
fp.section.display.title: Display
fp.section.display.desc: Information about your monitor or screen. These values are surprisingly unique and often help distinguish one device from another.
fp.section.gpu.title: Graphics card (GPU)
fp.section.gpu.desc: Information retrieved via WebGL. This data helps websites optimise graphics, but can also significantly contribute to identifying a specific device.
fp.section.network.title: Network
fp.section.network.desc: Data about your connection quality. Websites use it to optimise content, but it can also reveal your connection type.
fp.section.fingerprint.title: Unique fingerprint (SHA‑56)
fp.section.fingerprint.desc: The combination of all the above data creates a unique fingerprint of your device. It contains no personal data, but allows recognising a returning visit.
quishingIntro: These are not hypothetical threats. Here are documented real-world cases where a replaced or fake QR code cost people their money.
quishingSource: Sources: Radiozurnal / iROZHLAS (October 2024), The Bureau of Investigative Journalism (June 2025), Friends Against Scams UK, Action Fraud UK, Austin Transportation Department (2022), E15.cz (2021).
qc1title: Fake EasyPark stickers on parking meters
qc1text: Scammers covered parking meters in central Prague with pink stickers perfectly imitating EasyPark. Drivers paid the scammers instead of the city — and then also received a parking fine for non-payment.
qc1lessonText: Double hit: money lost + parking fine. Paying via QR code doesn't mean you've actually paid.
qc2text: Action Fraud received nearly 800 QR fraud reports in the 12 months to April 2025. Cases were reported at car parks in London, Cornwall, Plymouth, Scotland and Luton airport. The same criminal network operated in Canada and the US.
qc2lessonText: Average victim loss: hundreds of pounds. Fake stickers were replaced daily to evade detection.
qc3text: A woman scanned a QR code at Thornaby station — it looked like part of a legitimate information board. The fake page prompted her to enter payment details. Over £13,000 disappeared from her account (approx. 380,000 CZK).
qc3lessonText: A QR code in a public place looks completely normal — that's exactly why these scams are so effective.
qc4text: Scammers placed fake QR codes on more than 100 payment machines in San Antonio. In Austin, officials then checked 900 city meters and found fraudulent codes on 29 of them.
qc4lessonText: The scam scales easily — anyone can print a QR sticker for a few cents.
qc5title: Fake charity collection after South Moravia tornado
qc5text: After the South Moravia tornado, people wanted to help. A young man placed a fake QR code leading to his own account next to collection materials from Diecézní charity Brno. Fortunately, police caught him before anyone sent money. The case ended well — but the warning stands.
qc5lessonText: Police caught the perpetrator this time. But they might not next time. Always verify a charity QR code on the organisation's official website.
qc6text: Scammers replaced legitimate QR codes with fake ones across more than 200 locations of one retailer. Within 48 hours, damage control cost the company $2.3 million.
qc6lessonText: The scam doesn't only hurt victims — legitimate operators also suffer financial and reputational damage.
faq.q9: What is 'quishing' and has it actually happened?
faq.a9:
Quishing (QR + phishing) is an attack where a scammer covers or replaces a legitimate QR code with their own — which leads to a fake page instead of the real one.

It has really happened:

  • In the UK, Action Fraud received nearly 800 QR fraud reports in 12 months to April 2025 — victims lost a total of £3.5 million.
  • In Prague (2024), scammers covered parking meters with stickers imitating EasyPark.
  • In the Czech Republic after the tornado (2021), scammers placed fake QR codes next to charity collection materials.
  • In Texas, over 100 parking meters were covered with fraudulent codes.

How to protect yourself: Check whether the QR code looks like a sticker. Read the URL after scanning. For payments, verify the recipient before confirming.
qc7title: Fake QR codes on EV charging stations
qc7text: Scammers have started placing fake QR codes on EV charging points across Europe. A driver scans the code, enters card details on a fake page imitating the operator's interface — and charging never starts. Ubitricity confirmed attempts at fewer than 30 locations in Berlin. Czech ČEZ has also issued preventive warnings.
qc7lessonText: Charging stations with QR codes on a screen (not a sticker) are safer — a sticker can be covered, a screen cannot.
qc2source: Source: The Bureau of Investigative Journalism
